prompt: rgb.jpg is a horizontal strip of 5 frames, left to right in time order, sampled from the few seconds of a head-mounted (egocentric) video; the camera wearer is the viewpoint. depth.jpg, segmentation.jpg and pose.jpg are the same 5 frames rendered as a monocular depth map (brighter = nearer to the camera wearer), an instance segmentation map (coloured masks with class labels), and a body/hand skeleton map (yellow = body, magenta = hands) on black. Look at all four images. For EACH of the three maps, describe the spatial understanding that map supports, using the RGB strip for context: the layout of the scene; which people and objects are present and roughly how far each is from the camera wearer (in metres) and from each other; relative positions (left/right/in front/behind, above/below); which way people face and whether they look toward the camera wearer; what is within arm's reach of the camera wearer or of others; occlusions and anything partly out of view; and how these change across the 5 frames (approach, retreat, turning). Say what each map shows that is hard to see in the RGB alone, and where the map looks unreliable. Describe only spatial facts. Do not guess anyone's intentions, social norms, or what anyone should do. Return only JSON: {"depth": "...", "segmentation": "...", "pose": "..."} with 3-5 sentences each.

descriptions.depth: The depth map shows a top-down egocentric view where the camera wearer sits or crouches directly above a grey mechanical gearbox/axle assembly (~0.5–0.7 m below the camera, resting across their lap/legs) and in front of an elevated yellow mower deck (~0.6–1.2 m away, supported from below by a red jack stand on the concrete floor at ~1.3–1.5 m). Across the 5 frames, the camera wearer's arms and orange-gloved hands remain in the nearest foreground (~0.2–0.6 m, within immediate arm's reach), with the left arm lifting a long black drive shaft closer to the camera in frame 3 (brightest white, ~0.2–0.4 m) before extending forward to place it onto the left side of the yellow deck (~0.6–0.8 m) in frame 4 and retracting slightly in frame 5, while a second person standing to the front-left (~1.0–1.5 m away, ~0.3–0.5 m left of the mower deck, facing toward the mower/wearer with head cropped out of the top of the frame) becomes more visible in frames 3 and 4 as the camera tilts slightly upward and left before tilting back down in frame 5. The map clarifies the vertical layering that is harder to judge in RGB alone—specifically how the raised mower lip and side arms overhang the dark floor cavity and red jack stand by ~0.5 m, and how the lifted shaft in frame 3 rises well above the deck plane—while also showing the wearer's legs partially occluding the floor beneath the axle. However, the depth map is unreliable around thin structural rods on the front of the deck, inside dark shadowed recesses beneath the machine where details flatten to uniform black, and in frames 3–4 where the raised left arm saturates to pure white and merges depth-wise with the held shaft.
descriptions.segmentation: The segmentation map isolates only fragments of the scene against a black background, detecting the camera wearer's arms, hands, and lower torso/legs in the bottom foreground (~0.2–0.7 m away) and partially capturing the standing second person in the upper-left of frame 4 (~1.0–1.5 m away, facing the workspace from the left of the mower with their upper body cropped at the top border). Across the sequence, the wearer's two arms are merged into a single `person` mask with the torso in frame 1, split into two separate `person` instances at the bottom of frame 2 (~0.3 m apart), reduced to only the raised left arm in frame 3 as the right hand drops mostly out of view at the bottom edge, and erroneously merged with the standing bystander's torso/legs into one continuous pink `person` mask in frame 4 before splitting into separate left-arm and right-arm/lap `person` masks in frame 5. Although the map provides crisp boundary contours for the wearer's foreground limbs and highlights the spatial proximity where the outstretched left arm overlaps the bystander's silhouette in 2D projection during frame 4, it completely fails to segment the yellow mower deck, the green hammer resting on top of it (~0.8–1.0 m away), the handheld drive shaft, and the red jack stand, all of which are within or just beyond the wearer's and bystander's arm's reach. Furthermore, it is highly unreliable in class and instance assignment, misclassifying the central vertical metal gearbox housing (~0.6 m below the camera, between the wearer's knees) as a `bottle` in frames 4 and 5, missing the bystander entirely in frames 1–3 and 5, and fragmenting the camera wearer into multiple disconnected `person` instances.
descriptions.pose: The pose map renders only 2D magenta hand skeletons on a black background, detecting the camera wearer's orange-gloved hands within ~0.3–0.6 m in the lower foreground while completely omitting all yellow body skeletons for both the camera wearer and the standing person on the front-left (~1.0–1.5 m away). In frame 1, it locates the wearer's left hand in the lower-left corner (~0.5 m away, holding the shaft) and the raised right hand in the upper-right foreground (~0.3 m away); in frame 2, both hands appear near the bottom-left and bottom-center (~0.4–0.5 m away and ~0.15 m apart) near the axle assembly; in frame 3, only the lifted left hand is tracked near the center-left (~0.3 m away) while the right hand is largely out of view at the bottom border; in frame 4, no hands or bodies are detected at all even though the left hand is clearly placing the shaft onto the mower deck at ~0.7 m; and in frame 5, both hands reappear with the left hand above the axle (~0.4 m away) and the right hand lower-right (~0.5 m away). Compared to the RGB image alone, the articulated finger keypoints make it easier to see the exact curl, pinch posture, and facing orientation of the gloved fingers—such as the pinched thumb and index finger of the right hand in frame 1 and the inward-curled grip around the shaft in frame 3. However, the map is unreliable whenever hands are partially occluded by tools or angled away from the camera (completely missing the left hand in frame 4 and the partially visible right hand in frame 3), and it provides zero spatial information about full-body posture, the standing person's orientation, or the surrounding machinery.
